Word stress is predictable as is phrase stress when it is not being used for emphasis purposes. ... Within such phonological words, stress occurs on the last long vowel, or, in three-syllable words, on the first long vowel, or, if there is no long vowel, on the last diphthong, or, if there is no diphthong, on the penultimate syllable of the word. ... new_statements.quote: This being said, the glottal stop is still heard in stressed syllables, i.e. generally on the penultimate. Thus, the word ʻekaʻeka ‘to be happy’ is pronounced [e.ka.ʔeːka]: the glottal is silent word-initially, yet still audible under stress, correlated with the lengthening of the following vowel. [p. 95:] On the island of Hiva Oa (Marquesas), my elderly informants, who have been influenced very little by Tahitian, have maintained an original pronunciation, quite different from the phonetic rules of Tahitian. [...] When a lexeme is formed by reduplication, stress falls on the penultimate syllable: paepae ‘stone platform’ [pa.e.ˈpa.e]; tautau ‘suspend’ [ta.u.ˈta.u].
new_statements.translation: Authors' own French parallel, pp. 42-43: "On entend encore la consonne glottale lorsqu’elle se situe en position accentuée, c’est-à-dire généralement dans l’avant-dernière syllabe du mot. Ainsi, le mot ʻekaʻeka ‘être heureux’ se prononce [e.ka.ʔeːka] : tandis qu’à l’initiale la glottale est assourdie, elle est encore présente en position accentuée, et corrélée à l’allongement de la voyelle qui la suit. Dans l’île de Hiva Oa (Marquises), mes vieux informateurs très peu influencés par le tahitien ont su préserver une prononciation originale [...] Lorsqu’un lexème est formé d’une racine redoublée, l’accent tonique frappe l’avant-dernière syllable : paepae ‘plateforme de pierres’ [pa.e.ˈpa.e] ; tautau ‘suspendre’ [ta.u.ˈta.u]." (Orthographic forms paepae, tautau, ʻekaʻeka are set in a custom font whose text layer is garbled; they were read from the rendered page images.)
new_statements.citation: Charpentier, Jean-Michel & Alexandre François. 2015. Atlas linguistique de la Polynésie française. Berlin/Papeete: De Gruyter Mouton & UPF. 2562 pp.

Thus, the word [ʻekaʻeka] "to be happy" is pronounced [e.ka.ʔeːka]: the glottal is silent word-initially, yet still audible under [p.98 header "Organization and use of the Linguistic Atlas — 95"] stress, correlated with the lengthening of the following vowel.' and 'On the island of Hiva Oa (Marquesas), my elderly informants, who have been influenced very little by Tahitian, have maintained an original pronunciation, quite different from the phonetic rules…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists South Marquesan with an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies a placement (penultimate) with two transcribed examples plus the observation that the penult is where glottal stop and vowel lengthening are retained. Explicitly about the southern dialects (Hiva Oa, Tahuata, Fatu Hiva), examples from Hiva Oa, i.e. the right languoid for sout2866.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('generally on the penultimate'); the explicit placement statement is given for reduplicated lexemes (paepae [pa.e.ˈpa.e], tautau [ta.u.ˈta.u]) in the speech of elderly Hiva Oa speakers, where every vowel is a separate syllable (no diphthongs: totoua [to.to.u.a], nui [nu.i]), so the stressed penult is counted over vowel-syllables. Glottal stop survives only in the stressed (penultimate) syllable, where the following vowel is lengthened ([e.ka.ʔeːka]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated explicitly; the hedge 'generally on the penultimate' (généralement dans l'avant-dernière syllabe) implies non-penultimate cases exist but none are described. The authors note younger speakers, under Tahitian influence, now merge vowel sequences into diphthongs or insert glottals, which would change syllable counts; the remarks are phonetic observations in a dialect atlas, not a phonological analysis of stress.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress remarks describe the speech of elderly informants on Hiva Oa, and the glottal-stop observation names the southern Marquesan dialects (Hiva Oa, Tahuata, Fatu Hiva) as a group; both fall under South Marquesan (sout2866). The atlas's Marquesan survey points are Nuku Hiva, Ua Huka, Ua Pou (northern) and Hiva Oa, Tahuata, Fatu Hiva (southern); no stress statement is made for the northern dialects in this passage.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: both deciding passages (Lynch 2002:866; Mutu & Teikitutoua 2002:34-36 incl. fn.25) are verbatim in copies we hold, and the Mutu PDF is held in full. The weakness is languoid fit, not quotation: both sources describe North Marquesan (Nukuhiva, Ua Pou) and the record extends them to South Marquesan, for which Glottolog lists no grammar or phonology at all (Glottolog's most extensive descriptions Kruppa 1999, Ward 1962; Ward downloaded now and is silent on stress). The one South-specific statement I could locate and open, Charpentier & François 2015 Atlas intro pp.94-95 (Fr. 42-43), says for Hiva Oa that stress is 'generally on the penultimate', that vowel sequences are heterosyllabic ([to.to.u.a], [nu.i]) and that reduplications stress the penultimate syllable ([pa.e.ˈpa.e], [ta.u.ˈta.u]); it shows a lengthened stressed penult ([e.ka.ʔeːka]) but says nothing about final long vowels attracting stress.
